# Universal Mapping Property of a Representable Contravariant Functor

## Setup

Let $F: \mathcal{C} \to \text{Set}$ be a contravariant functor (equivalently, a covariant functor $F: \mathcal{C}^{\text{op}} \to \text{Set}$). The functor is **representable** if there exists an object $X \in \text{ob}(\mathcal{C})$ together with a natural isomorphism

$$\xi: \text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(-, X) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} F.$$

Here $\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(-, X): \mathcal{C}^{\text{op}} \to \text{Set}$ is the contravariant hom-functor represented by $X$.

## The Universal Element

From the natural isomorphism $\xi$, evaluate the component at $X$ itself on the identity morphism:

$$x := \xi_X(\text{id}_X) \in F(X).$$

This element $x \in F(X)$ is called the **universal element** of the representation.

## The Universal Mapping Property

**Theorem.** The pair $(X, \xi)$ — equivalently, the pair $(X, x)$ with $x = \xi_X(\text{id}_X)$ — satisfies the following universal property:

> For every object $C \in \mathcal{C}$ and every element $y \in F(C)$, there exists a **unique** morphism $f: C \to X$ in $\mathcal{C}$ such that
> $$F(f)(x) = y.$$

## Proof

**Existence.** Let $C \in \mathcal{C}$ and $y \in F(C)$. Since $\xi_C: \text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(C, X) \to F(C)$ is a bijection (being a component of a natural isomorphism), there exists a unique $f \in \text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(C, X)$ with $\xi_C(f) = y$.

It remains to show $\xi_C(f) = F(f)(x)$. By naturality of $\xi$ applied to the morphism $f: C \to X$ (viewed in $\mathcal{C}^{\text{op}}$ as $f^{\text{op}}: X \to C$), the following square commutes:

$$\require{AMScd}
\begin{CD}
\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, X) @>{\xi_X}>> F(X) \\
@V{f \circ -}VV @V{F(f)}VV \\
\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(C, X) @>{\xi_C}>> F(C)
\end{CD}$$

Chasing $\text{id}_X$ through the diagram:

- Top-right path: $\text{id}_X \xmapsto{\xi_X} x \xmapsto{F(f)} F(f)(x)$.
- Left-bottom path: $\text{id}_X \xmapsto{f \circ -} f \xmapsto{\xi_C} \xi_C(f)$.

Commutativity gives $F(f)(x) = \xi_C(f) = y$. $\checkmark$

**Uniqueness.** Suppose $f, g: C \to X$ both satisfy $F(f)(x) = y = F(g)(x)$. By the same naturality argument, $\xi_C(f) = F(f)(x) = y = F(g)(x) = \xi_C(g)$. Since $\xi_C$ is injective, $f = g$. $\checkmark$

## Converse (Equivalence)

Conversely, if there exists an object $X$ and an element $x \in F(X)$ such that for every $C$ and every $y \in F(C)$ there is a unique $f: C \to X$ with $F(f)(x) = y$, then the assignment

$$\xi_C: \text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(C, X) \to F(C), \qquad f \mapsto F(f)(x)$$

is a bijection (by existence and uniqueness), and naturality in $C$ follows directly from the functoriality of $F$. Hence $\xi: \text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(-, X) \xrightarrow{\sim} F$ is a natural isomorphism, and $F$ is representable with universal element $x = \xi_X(\text{id}_X)$.

## Summary

The universal mapping property of the representing pair $(X, \xi)$ is:

> **For every object $C \in \mathcal{C}$ and every $y \in F(C)$, there exists a unique morphism $f: C \to X$ such that $F(f)(\xi_X(\text{id}_X)) = y$.**

Equivalently, the map $\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(C, X) \to F(C)$ given by $f \mapsto F(f)(x)$ is a bijection, natural in $C$. The element $x = \xi_X(\text{id}_X) \in F(X)$ is the universal element, and every element of $F(C)$ is obtained uniquely by "pulling back" the universal element along a unique morphism into $X$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
